title: Global Fishing Watch data lets Kiribati fine a vessel US$1 million for fishing in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area
summary: Kiribati used the Google-Oceana-SkyTruth platform to document Marshalls 203 fishing illegally in PIPA; a US$1 million fine plus a US$1 million goodwill grant followed (reported September 2016).
account: Global Fishing Watch, developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google, launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. It processes AIS tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Before launch, the Washington Post reported, the government of Kiribati used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally. That was inside the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, declared off-limits to commercial fishing in early 2015, resulting in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of GDP. The sources on file do not date the fine, so the date is that of the first report.
purpose: Make commercial fishing activity visible in near real time by processing AIS vessel tracks to identify when vessels are fishing.
system: Global Fishing Watch (AIS-based fishing detection using machine learning)
taxonomy_note: Loose fit; the criminal activity penalized is illegal fishing in a protected area, and the fine is the only documented outcome.

ratings.reason: Kiribati secured a US$1 million fine against Central Pacific Fishing Company plus a US$1 million goodwill grant (Grist). The BBC piece puts the total at US$2 million, about 1% of the country's GDP.
No source documents subsequent fishing pressure or deterrence inside the protected area.

ai_role.statement: An independent newspaper confirms that Kiribati used the platform to document the illegal operation. Oceana describes the platform's fishing detection as machine learning over AIS data. No source on file says whether the classifier's output, as opposed to the vessel's track, carried the case. Developer (Oceana, SkyTruth, Google) and deployer (Kiribati) are distinct.

later.note: In June 2017 Indonesia became the first country to publish its proprietary vessel monitoring system data through Global Fishing Watch, adding nearly 5,000 vessels to the platform, with Peru announcing it would follow.
later.quote: This week, at the United Nation’s Ocean Conference, the Republic of Indonesia becomes the first nation ever to publish Vessel Monitoring System (VMS) data revealing the location and activity of its commercial fishing fleet.
